Right Hon. 'J. L. ILSLEY (Acting Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, discussions of the world food situation have taken place over the week-end between members of the Canadian government and Mr. Herbert Morrison, M.P., Lord President of the Council, of the United * Kingdom, who came to Ottawa for this purpose following similar discussions with United States representatives in Washington at which the Canadian ambassador was present.
The Canadian government has taken note of the joint statement issued by the United Kingdom and the United States on May 17, following Mr. Morrison's discussions in Washington and has expressed general agreement with the proposals it contains for continuing consultation and collaboration to meet the world food crisis.
During the discussions in Ottawa the steps already taken by Canada and the United Kingdom to alleviate the disastrous effects of world food shortages were reviewed and broad lines of future policy were discussed.
The maximum supplies of bread grains that are at present likely to be available from May through to September, 1946 have been assessed at some ten million tons, of which Canada expects to supply 2-3 million tons. Screened requirements for the same period were expected to total 13-4 million tons leaving a deficiency of 3-4 million tons or about 25 per
cent. A further intensive review and scaling down of these requirements to the barest minimum needs are likely to reduce the gap over this five-months period to something under one million tons. Inevitably severe hardship will result and great danger of famine will continue. The Canadian government has agreed to associate itself with the United Kingdom and the United States governments in maintaining constant review of the situation, and to put forth its best efforts to secure and make available additional supplies of grain.
The Canadian ministers described the comprehensive programme of agricultural production and of conservation of food which their government is carrying out to meet this situation. In anticipation of the urgent world need for food that would arise immediately following the conclusion of the war, Canadian food production had been expanded during the war years. This high rate of expanded production has been maintained and in some cases even increased. Wheat acreage has been raised to a very high level. Rationing and restrictions on sales of certain foods to help provide more for export were continued and even extended; meat rationing was reimposed. Complete control of agricultural products, in particular grains, has been retained in order to ensure that as much food as possible may be made available to the hungry of other nations.
When, some months ago, it became apparent that the expected serious food situation in the world would be greatly aggravated by drought in large areas, and by other difficulties, the Canadian government took still further steps to meet the threat of famine. On March 17 the Prime Minister announced a nine-point programme upon which the Canadian government had decided in order to increase supplies of foodstuffs for export. This programme included:
1.	Reduction by 10 per cent below 1945 of wheat released for human consumption in Canada.
2.	Reduction by 50 per cent of wheat released for distilleries.
3.	Special income tax arrangements to encourage immediate marketing of wheat stored on farms.
4.	Measures to release increased quantities of oats and No. 4 wheat for export.
5.	Special priorities for rail transport of wheat for export.
6.	Modification of regulations affecting bulk shipment of flour and feed.
7.	A campaign to urge Canadian farmers to plan their production to obtain the maximum yield of foodstuffs over the next four years.
Food-World Shortage

8.	A campaign for the reduction of inventories of wheat and wheat products.
9.	A campaign to encourage consumer savings, avoidance of waste, and development of home gardens.
This programme has been put into effect and is already producing encouraging results. Other special action has also been taken by the government. For example, further wheat is being diverted from producers of both potable and industrial alcohol to the extent that substitutes become available; additional efforts to reduce use of wheat for animal feeds are being made.
The United Kingdom representatives described the efforts being put forth in the United Kingdom. Consumer rationing has been continued and over a wide field rations are now below low wartime levels. The rations of home-based United Kingdom forces have been reduced. The extraction rate of flour has been raised several times and will be maintained at 90 per cent during the critical May to September period. Supplies of grain for distilling have been cut from 300,000 tons to
130,000	tons. The size of loaves has been reduced, while production of biscuits, cakes and pastry has been substantially curtailed. Beer production has been set at 90 per cent of prewar production. Cereal production is being encouraged and a number of special directions and inducements have recently been introduced to this end. Feeding of millable wheat to live stock remains prohibited and rations for livestock have been cut down. Consumers are being encouraged to conserve food and to reduce waste.
Further, the United Kingdom has recently agreed to forego another 200,000 tons of imports which will thus be released for use elsewhere. This has been done with full awareness of the dangers to the United Kingdom in the way of still further interruptions of distribution or restrictions on the austere diet obtaining in the United Kingdom for the six years since the beginning of the war.
The Canadian and United Kingdom governments agree that every effort must be put forth to remove completely the threat of world famine, a threat which will continue at least until the harvests of 1947 become available. The two governments agree that they will continue to collaborate through the combined food board or other appropriate agencies to this end. They will continue to consult on measures of major importance which may be found necessary to meet the present world food shortage.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am aware that the statement which the Acting Prime Minister

has just made is not supposed to be debatable, but perhaps the house would permit me to make one or two observations.
I want to commend the government for this announcement, and for its plan for further consultation and cooperation in this crisis with the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States. I can see no harm in the minister's restatement of the government's policy with respect to increasing the supply of food under these circumstances. I might just point out in passing, however, that when the minister says the Canadian people have put in a higher acreage of wheat in recent years, that has not been done because of, but rather in spite of, government policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a point of order, is this debatable?

The statement made by the Acting Prime Minister is not debatable. It has been the practice, however, to permit the leader of the opposition to ask certain questions. I have always been generous in that respect, but I cannot permit any debate.

Mr. Speaker, you did permit the Acting Prime Minister to make a very important statement. I now ask Your Honour: Are you going to deny me the opportunity of commenting upon it? If you are, I take my seat.

As I have already said, it is well known practice in the house that statements made by ministers at this stage of the proceedings, are not debatable. I thought it was my duty to permit the leader of the opposition to ask certain questions, or to ask for information, but I cannot permit debate.

I was not proposing to debate the subject at all, I had simply intended to make some comments. The only comment I have made thus far is to deny what the minister has said, namely that as a result of government policy the acreage of wheat in this country has been increased. The only other thing I wish to say is this: The leader of the house has referred to the fact that a member of the United Kingdom government is in Canada to-day to discuss this very important matter of food for a hungry world. The minister stated that he had met certain members of the government. My question is this: Would the government be good enough to arrange that that representative from the United Kingdom government meet representatives of other parties, as well as those supporting the government? We would all like to see him and to have his story and, so far as possible, we would like to support his request. The minister has already intimated

subtopic: BANK OF CANADA-MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC DEBT
speechtext:
1.	Nil.
2.	Yes.
3.	The Bank of Canada acts as fiscal agent of the dominion, government without charge

in accordance with the provisions of section 23 (1) of the Bank of Canada Act. These fiscal agency duties include, in addition to management of the public debt, the distribution of subsidiary coin; shipment of gold to world markets for sale; purchasing, selling and safekeeping of securities for government departments and agencies; and maintenance of government deposit accounts. The Bank of Canada also performs the normal functions of a central bank which include the tendering of advice on financial and monetary matters to the government of the country in which it is located.

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TRADESMEN'S STRIKE-COMPLETION OP BUILDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for giving me advance notice of his two questions. His first question relates to a strike of plasterers and cement finishers at Sunnybrook hospital. The facts are as follows:
On Wednesday, the 8th of. May, the regional war labour board awarded to the union plasterers of Toronto an amount of $1.30 per hour, which was 5 cents per hour less than had been requested. This award represented an increase of 9 cents per hour and it was * effective from May 1, 1946. On Friday, the 17th, the plasterers in the Toronto area laid off work and held a meeting, the results of which were that they requested from the different contractors in the Toronto area, in addition to the raise already granted by the regional war labour board on the 8th instant, holidays with pay for each of the eight statutory holidays observed throughout the year.
At noon to-day, the plasterers' union, which represents 600 plasterers, notified the plastering contractors that they were on strike asking for these holidays with pay. At a meeting of the plastering contractors held at 12 o'clock to-day, the four major contractors refused the demands but five minor contractors accepted them and their men may be at work. The results of this will not be known until tomorrow.
The regional war labour board have today granted increases, effective May 1, to the following trades: bricklayers, to $1.35 per hour; lathers, same as increased rate for plasterers, $1.30 per hour; plumbers and steam-fitters, to $1.27 per hour; sheet metal workers, to $1.28 per hour.
Just before coming into the house, Mr. MacNamara, the deputy minister of labour, advised me that he had received a telephone call from the Toronto labour exchange to the effect that they expected this strike would be settled during the week.

My hon. friend's second question related to the completion of the work at Sunnybrook hospital. I would not dare to fix a date, right in the midst of the strike, when the hospital will be completed, but I am ready to give a progress report on that project, as follows:
Boiler House. Completed and in operation.
Neuro-psychiatric Building. Practically completed. Expect occupation by June 15.
Up-patients Building. Expect occupation by October 15.
Active treatment building. About 95 per cent of all the concrete in floors and roof slabs has been placed. Exterior wall work is about 65 per cent completed. Plumbing, heating and ventilating pipes and electric conduits are being installed, and some tile partition work has been done m basement and on ground floor.
Out-patient building. Concrete in all floors will be placed by May 4-
This report is dated April 30.
-leaving only the roof and penthouse slabs to be done. Exterior stonework at ground floor is about 40 per cent completed.
O. & S.A. and maintenance building. All walls, columns and concrete work on ground floor are finished, and structural steel framework is about 20 per cent erected.
Laundry. All footings and walls, necessary for erection of structural steel framework, have been finished; and forms for main floor concrete slab are ready for placing of concrete.
Emergency water and coal storage. This structure is completed.
Services. As previously reported, power water and sewer lines are all finished, and generally m use. No road work has been done since last fall.
Bed Cross lodge. This building should be completed about May 31.

Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of bill No. 16, respecting the manufacture, testing, sale, storage and importation of explosives.
He said: The Explosives Act of Canada, 1914, chapter 31, was introduced in 1911 and passed by parliament on June 12, 1914, under the Honourable Mr. Coderre, but its proclamation was-deferred until after the war of 1914-18. The act is based upon the British act of 1875, which is the general basis of the explosives acts of South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Belgium and other countries. It has not been changed in any respect since 1920, the year in which it was proclamed, save for the general revision of Canadian statutes in 1927.
Revision of the Explosives Act has been under consideration for some time and a revision has now been prepared by the Department of Justice in consultation with officers of the mines and geology branch. The amendments proposed are largely minor in nature, and are the results of, first, experience in the administration of the act, and second, administrative changes in the department.
Five important changes have been made. First, the governor in council will have authority to make regulations respecting the sale of explosives; second, provision is made for forfeiture to the crown of any unauthorized explosive in respect of which a conviction has been obtained; third, an inspector may seize and detain an explosive which he believes is not authorized; fourth, the minister will have authority to seize and destroy abandoned or deteriorated explosives which have become a public danger; fifth, servants of the crown, excepting the Department of National Defence, are to be brought within the application of the act.
During the twenty-five years of operation the act has proved its value and demonstrated the desirability of having control over explosives which may be put on the market and of regulating the conditions with regard to safety under which explosives a-re manufactured and stored. Regulations for the more effective application of the act were made. These deal with such matters as the classification of explosives and the testing and'examina-tion before being declared an authorized explosive. The effect has been beneficial, and in their administration manufacturers of explosives have given excellent cooperation, with

Explosives Act
the result that quality and uniformity of explosives have undoubtedly improved to the advantage of the user.
The quantity of explosives manufactured yearly has increased steadily. Production of commercial explosives in 1919, the year preceding the proclamation of the act, was slightly over twenty-one million pounds; the greatest production was in 1940 when it totalled over eighty-four million pounds, a four-fold increase. Despite the great increase in production the number of accidents has shown a steady decline. Entire freedom from accident can scarcely be looked for in any industry; still less so in the one which involves the risks which are ever present to those engaged in work of explosives, but much can and is being done to reduce the known hazards.
Rules for factories and magazines and regulations for the packing and transportation of explosives, otherwise than by railway, were made under authority of the act. Rules, of necessity, are of a general nature intended to apply to explosives plants of various kinds manufacturing different types of explosives, but their object is primarily intended to express what is recognized to be good practice in the manufacture, storage and handling of explosives.
By order in council P.C. 191/1365 of fourteenth June, 1932, all officers, non-commissioned officers and constables of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, while serving on that force, are appointed deputy inspectors of explosives without pay. Members of the force have rendered valuable assistance in the administration of the Explosives Act in many sections of Canada, particularly in the inaccessible areas such as the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
Soon after the outbreak of war it was deemed advisable in the public interest to control the possession, sale and use of explosives. There was no authority under the Explosives Act to regulate these; consequently recourse was had to the War Measures Act under which order in council P.C. 2903, July 4, 1940, was passed. This order in council, during the years it has been in force, has proved satisfactory and has been well received by both vendors and purchasers of explosives. It has proved a useful measure to peace officers through keeping them fully informed of all purchases of explosives, with the result that sabotage by the use of commercial explosives was practically unknown in Canada during the war years.
Experience gained in administering P.C. 2903 indicates that in the interest of public safety some measure of control-not provided
in the present Explosives Act-over the operations of retail dealers who store for sale small quantities of explosives should be continued in the post-war period. For this purpose the bill now being considered will restrict the sale of blasting explosives to the owner or operator of a licensed factory, licensed magazine or registered premises. The advantages of this provision from the viewpoint of public safety and administration will be:
1.	All vendors will be obliged-to make known
.their dealings in explosives.	,
2.	Premises, other than licensed magazines, in which explosives are stored for sale will be subject to periodic inspection to ensure that the terms of the licence or certificate- are being fully observed.
3.	Records of sale of explosives which vendors are obliged to maintain would, as in the past, assist peace officers in the enforcement of law.
Order in council P.C. 2903 requires purchasers of explosives to obtain an explosives purchase permit. This restriction is not provided for in the revision of the act and will be discontinued when the new act is passed.
The present Explosives Act does not provide adequately for the disposal of unauthorized, abandoned, and deteriorated explosives. The bill seeks to correct this omission by providing authority, when warranted, to seize, forfeit, and dispose of unauthorized explosives and explosives which have been abandoned or have become deteriorated and a danger to the public.
To summarize, the new act continues the controls of the old act over the manufacture, testing, storage, and importation of explosives, and in addition requires that all who sell explosives shall register their premises. This bill has been before the other chamber and was passed almost without alteration. It was drawn in conjunction with the Justice department in the light of the experience gained during the war, and it is thought that in its present form it will be adequate to take care of the dangers of explosives and give added powers for the protection of the public. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I move the second reading of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, if the bill will achieve all that the minister has just set out, it ought to be worth while, but I understood from what he said that an act containing much of what is in this bill has been on the statute books for some time.
I rise to support any legislation or any programme at all which will strengthen the hands of whoever is charged with the control of the sale of explosives and prevent any such disaster as occurred in Toronto a week ago Sunday night. It passes my comprehension how four young lads could go into a store-I presume

Explosives Act

on College street, Toronto, because the accident happened on College street near Clinton street-purchase powerful explosives and take them out on the street-car tracks and set them off, with the result that a young man of nineteen years of age was struck on the head with a rocket and his skull pierced, resulting in his death a few hours afterwards. I should like to read for the benefit of the members what the Toronto police said about these rockets, one of which killed this young man. I have not the date of the clipping, but it must have been about May 13 or 14 last: Police say that the rockets, which were purchased by the boys at a nearby store, were of a powerful variety.
I should like to know how any young lads could buy such a powerful rocket. What control was there over the store in which these rockets were purchased? What control was there over the sale of these rockets to the merchant? I presume the bill will cover all that, and if it does, it will be a step in the right direction. Continuing with the clipping: The boys laid them lengthwise on the streetcar tracks, and when they were fired they shot along the groove in the rail. Some of the rockets were reported to have travelled as far as Bathurst street in this manner, a distance of five blocks.
One can picture what would have happened had anyone been in the line of fire five blocks away from where the rockets were set off. I hope that the new act will prevent the recurrence of such accidents. The article continues:
Announcing steps to prevent recurrence of such fatalities, Inspector Frank Crowe said that police officials would confer with Crown Attorney J. W. McFadden, to-day to discuss a Toronto by-law which forbids the setting off of fireworks in the city.
"A by-law regarding the exploding of fireworks is still on the books," he said. "Rockets of the type used Sunday are not playthings, but are dangerous weapons in the hands of grown-ups, let alone juveniles."
I hope that the provisions of this bill will prevent the recurrence of such a disaster. I nope that it will control the sale of powerful rockets by the manufacturer to the wholesaler, and by the wholesaler .to the street merchant, and that it will prevent the street corner merchant from selling rockets to juveniles who go out and set them off on the streei in this manner.
I might mention another incident which occurred near where I live. A young lad went, into a store to buy some small ammunition for an air gun. The storekeeper refused to sell it to him on account of his age, and so the boy got an older person in the store to buy it for him. I hope this bill will prevent that kind of thing. Too many people are

being injured through these small, supposedly harmless firearms. Certainly the firing of rockets on streets should be prevented by every means. Steps should be taken to prevent their sale to juveniles and to control their sale to merchants.

Mr. Speaker, the matter just dealt with by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) was one which I had intended to bring to the attention of the house. So far as I can see, the bill, aa was stated by the minister, is merely a restatement of the British Explosives Act, together with a revision of the Canadian Explosives Act, bringing it up to date and applying statutory form to the orders in council which were passed during the war.
So far as the general purport is concerned, there can be no argument. It is really a photographic copy of the original Explosives Act brought up to date in order to remedy any defects which have been revealed .in practical experience. But consideration should be given to including in this bill sky-rockets and firecrackers of the type referred to by the hon. member for Davenport. I have read over the bill and I can find in it no section which in any way would be applicable to what was mentioned by my hon. friend.
If I might be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to refer to just one section of the bill, section 2(c), which defines "explosive", it includes "fireworks, fuses, rockets, percussion caps, detonators, cartridges, ammunition of all descriptions." But in view of the use of the words and the order in which they appear I should think that fireworks, fuses, rockets, would have to do in general with fireworks, fuses and rockets similar in action to percussion caps, detonators, cartridges, railway track torpedoes, fuses and other signals. In other words, there is established in that section a type or a genus, which would make the section inapplicable under the circumstances detailed by the hon. member for Davenport, and I am sure it would be the wish of the house and of the minister that there should be the fullest possible control of explosives. This bill will not cover a control which is vitally necessary to-day; I refer to firearms, which are all too frequently used. It is intended to go part way, and I am sure it would be the wish of the house that it go as far as possible to prevent the recurrence of such an event as has been described and to remove from the hands of young men, too large a percentage of whom are launching on a career of crime, opportunities of securing firearms, which are not only required in

Explosives Act
ordinary business pursuits but are part of the stock in trade of persons engaged in nefarious practices.
I have read the bill carefully and compared it with the British act and with the orders in council to which the minister made reference. I am happy to say that it gives evidence of unusual care in preparation and draftsmanship, and the other house in which it was introduced, deserves a measure of credit for the attention it has paid to the bill. May I add that this is a challenge to the commons-to the government *-in any event in that much legislation of this kind which is introduced in the commons might well- be initiated in the other house, where they have a great deal more leisure and more opportunities of examination. The bill as it stands shows what can be done when there is proper cooperation between the two houses of parliament. There is a care and directness in draftsmanship in the bill which is too often lacking, and it indicates the desirability of using to the limit the experience and the facilities which the other house offers for considered legislation.

The hon. member for Davenport was referring to an accident which recently took place; and I have also in mind the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre. In section 2,
(c) "explosive" means gunpowder, blasting powder, nitroglycerine, gun-cotton, dynamite, blasting gelatine, gelignite, fulminates of mercury or of other metals, coloured fires, and every other substance made, manufactured or used with a view to produce a violent effect by explosion, or pyrotechnic effect, and includes fireworks, fuses, rockets, percussion caps, detonators, cartridges, ammunition of all descriptions, railway track torpedoes, fusees and other signals, and every other adaptation or preparation of any such substance;
I would imagine that that definition of "explosive" would cover what the hon. member for Davenport has spoken of. In the report he read I think the word "rockets" was used, and that word is included in this interpretation of "explosive". Section 4 provides that regulations shall be made "respecting the sale of explosives". Subsection 1 reads that 63260-107J
"The Governor in Council may make regulations___(n) respecting the sale of explosives."
That clause was inserted for the purpose of having some record by those who sell explosives of whom they sell to. During the war provision was made that those purchasing explosives should go to a magistrate or justice of the peace or mayor of a town in order to obtain ammunition. Exception to this was taken by a good many people throughout the country, who complained of the inconvenience they had to undergo. Sometimes it involved a journey of twenty or thirty miles. It is thought that by regulations made under this clause, which was not in the former act, provision could be made whereby those who are selling explosives will keep a record of those to whom they are selling, and of the amount sold, and thus there will be some check on the sale of explosives. I do not know whether that fully answers the question of the hon. member for Davenport, but I take it that it covers to some extent the inquiry of the hon. member for Lake Centre with regard to the sale of rockets, or of ammunition as referred to by the hon. member.

Is it the opinion of the law officers of the crown that section 2, subparagraph (c), and the one to which the minister just had reference, would cover a case such as was referred to by the hon. member for Davenport? If he has that assurance, then the responsibility has been discharged.

This accident occurred so recently that I had no occasion to inquire of the law officers with regard to it, but this section was drafted for the very purpose, and contains the power to accomplish exactly what the hon. member for Davenport desires. It would cover any explosive which would create an accident, including such an accident as that to which the hon. member has referred.

The minister says that the clause as at present constituted was drafted to cover just such cases, among others, as mentioned by the hon. member. As a matter of fact the old section read exactly the same, and in the explanatory notes, paragraph
(c), as set out, "explosive" includes fireworks, fuses, rockets, percussion caps, detonators, cartridges, and ammunition of all descriptions. The old section as it stood-and I think I am correct in this-did not cover the condition of affairs referred to by the hon. member for Davenport, and if it did not, then certainly the amendments now suggested would not cover it since those amendments merely substitute, for "fog and other signals", railway track torpedoes, fusees and other signals. That is the only alteration in that section. I would suggest that if it is the -minister's wish, as

apparently it is, that this measure should cover the sale and disposal of rockets and also firecrackers of a dangerous type, a submission should be made to the law officers, to ascertain whether or not, as at present constituted, the section would cover that type of thing; if not, then the committee could suggest an amendment to the section. No. Those are under the department of defence.
Under what section?

Those are under the control of the department of defence, not under this act. Ordinary fuses that might be used on the

railway would come under this act, but those that my hon. friend speaks of are under the control of the department of defence.

But they may not be under the control of the defence department. They might be under the control of the Department of Munitions and Supply. Section 3 states:
This act shall apply to the possession, storing, sale or offering for sale, making, manufacture or importation of explosives by or on behalf of His Majesty in right of Canada or any province except explosives under the direction or control of the Minister of National Defence.
There ma3' be explosives that belong to the dominion government but are not under the direction or control of the Minister of National Defence. For example, explosives may be under the control of the Department of Munitions and Supply. In that case, does the word "fuses" in line 14 of 2 (c) apply, or is that word limited to fireworks?

I am informed that fuzes, from the military point of view, are not spelt in the same way. These fuses would cover in the last sentence what calls for "every other adaptation or preparation of any such substance". Does that meet the hon. member's point?

I must confess that I am a little puzzled about the matter. It might be given a little more consideration. The minister said he was going to refer this section back to the law officers and perhaps he might consider this point.

I must say that I thought, when I read over this provision, "railway track torpedoes, fusees and other signals, and every other adaptation or preparation of any such substance", it would be wide enough to cover all that the hon. gentleman has in mind. However, we are allowing this to stand over and I will consider what he says.
The minister says it does not include fuzes under the control of the Department of National Defence.
It does not apply to explosives of any kind under the charge of the Department of National Defence.
Then does it include explosives under the control of the Department of Munitions and Supply?
Certainly I would say it would apply to those, unquestionably.

I should like to pursue a little farther the case I mentioned a few moments ago. I understood the hon. member for Lake Centre to say he had thoroughly

Explosives Act
read this bill. I have read it casually, but not thoroughly. He also said he had carefully read the British act, and could not find in it any clause that would cover the case I brought up. What I want to suggest to the minister is that in the preparation of the regulations, they should prevent the sort ot thing that took place in Toronto a week or ten days ago, when four young lads were able to purchase very powerful explosives in the form of rockets. I believe the regulations should prevent the sale of such rockets by any wholesaler for resale to comer stores, hardware stores or anyone else, where boys or juveniles might purchase them. To the extent humanly possible will the regulations under this act prevent the producer of such high explosives from selling them to, let us say, a wholesaler, and will they prevent the wholesaler from selling them to the small corner stores which in turn will sell them to juveniles? In this case a young man, nineteen or twenty years old, with all his life before him, was killed. He was minding his own business when from down the street, some distance away, a rocket came and punctured his skull, so that he died a day or two later. If that racket had been fired by an adult I presume it would be a case of manslaughter. I do not know whether these boys should be punished, particularly, but I believe there should be some control over the sale of such powerful explosives to young lads. Will this act prevent that sort of thing?

The hon. gentleman is referring -to a newspaper report concerning an accident which apparently involved a rocket. That is covered by the interpretation clause, which includes rockets. Then the hon. member asks if there is power under the act to prevent the sale of such explosives. When we come to section 4 he will find that regulations can be made under paragraph (n) with respect to the sale of explosives, and in the making of these regulations account will be taken of what the hon. gentleman has said, in order that the sale of explosives may be as closely guarded as possible. No one, of course, can provide entirely against the possibility of accident, but there is power in the act to make rules and regulations respecting the sale of explosives. That is one of the new features of this bill as compared with previous legislation.

Would the minister explain exactly the position we shall be in after the passage of the bill with respect to Canadian Arsenals Limited? I do not think it can be said that Canadian Arsenals Limited will be under the direction and control of the Minister of National Defence. It will be a
crown company which will produce almost all, if not all, the explosives required by the services, and I am quite doubtful whether under this act the inspectors charged with enforcing the act will have the opportunity or will be required to inspect the operations of Canadian Arsenals Limited.

We are not dealing with that now, but still from the general point of view section 6 provides that the minister may issue licences for factories and magazines. Crown companies will have to have their licences, the same as any other institutions. Then power is given under sections 17 and following with regard to the powers of the inspectors to enter into any factory, magazine or premises where explosives may be manufactured or stored. So .. that I think the point raised by the hon. gentleman has been pretty well covered in these three sections, and perhaps we might deal with them when we reach them.

Does the minister know whether the rocket which was involved in the accident in Toronto was of Canadian or Chinese manufacture? The reason I am asking is that in a store on Sparks street they have fireworks which have been manufactured in China, and I wondered if the rockets in question had been of Chinese or Canadian manufacture. Another reason I asked is that one of the'largest manufacturers of fireworks on this continent, if not the largest, generally sell fireworks or rockets for large displays direct to fairs or municipalities, and they generally send out to look after those displays men who understand these fireworks and can look after them properly. I do not think our Canadian firms would sell, to the general public rockets which would cause such damage.
The information we have with regard to the rockets involved in this accident is that they were made in Canada.

I suppose the minister does not know what size they were, whether they were half-pound, one pound or two-pound. There is another type of fireworks which is equally dangerous; what they call mortars. These fire shells weighing a pound or two, and if they are not handled by an expert the person firing them is likely to have his head blown off, because they fire instantly.

As I understand the act, the minister has complete control over all explosives used in connection with mining operations. This is an important matter in Nova Scotia, since explosives are used in coal and other mining. Recently in one of the coal mines there was a complaint
Explosives Act

that the explosives were defective, and that owing to delayed explosions the workmen were subjected to additional hazards, to such an extent that they refused to continue to work in this mine until an investigation had been made. As I follow the discussion to-day, the minister has full responsibility for-the quality and handling of such explosives. Could he tell the committee the result of that investigation; whether these explosives were defective and, if not, whether reassurance was given the men working in this mine in Nova Scotia that they could return to their work in safety? We realize that coal miners and other miners are subject to great hazards in the carrying out of their work, and they ought not to be subjected to hazards arising through defective explosives or defective machinery.
I understand the hon. member to say that an accident took place in one of the Nova Scotia mines.

Owing to what was described as delayed explosives, thereby creating a hazard for coal miners which prompted them to refuse to continue operations until a thorough investigation had been made. Has the minister a report respecting such investigations, and will the men be given some reassurance?

I am informed that the accident was never brought to the attention of the department. It will be noted that section 2 (h) describes "magazine" as:
. . . any building, storehouse, structure or place in which any explosive is kept or stored, but does not include
(i) a place at or in and for the use of a mine or quarry in a province in which provision is made by the law of such province for the efficient inspection of mines and quarries and explosives used in connection therewith.
The use of the explosives will be subject to inspection by provincial departments. In this instance I suggest it was the use of the explosives which caused the accident, a matter which would be within the jurisdiction of the province. We provide only the places in which it can be used, subject always, of course, to the jurisdiction of the provinces in that connection.

I understand the minister's department assumes no responsibility for defective explosives in the hands of coal miners. The explosion to which I referred in Nova Scotia resulted in the shutting down of a mine for I do not know how many days at a time when the production of coal is required to as great an extent as has ever obtained in the history of our country
[Mr. P. C. Black.1

When we reach it I shall direct the hon. member's attention particularly to section 26 in the bill which provides:
Nothing in this act shall relieve any person of the obligation to comply with the requirements of any licence law, or other law or bylaw of any province or municipality, lawfully enacted, with regard to the storage, handling, sale or other dealing with explosives, nor of any liability or penalty imposed by such law or by-law for any violation thereof.

That may be all right, but I want to know if the minister and his department are responsible for defective explosives in the hands of coal miners. If the explosives were not defective, then all I ask is some reassurance of that fact. But if they were, I want to know if the minister's department is responsible for their use in this instance.

The manufacture of explosives, under this measure, is a procedure for which the department would be responsible. The use of the explosives in a province, or in the mines of a province, would be subject to its jurisdiction, and to its laws in that connection. This department, is responsible for the making or manufacture, but not for the use.

Do I gather from what the minister has said that the use of explosives is entirely within the jurisdiction of provincial governments? I have in mind the use of dynamite, which is mentioned in section 2 (c) of the bill? I have in mind particularly the careless way in which dynamite is handed out by certain quarry operators to people who are using explosives for different purposes. Is there anything in the bill to restrict the handling of explosives, and dynamite in particular? I know it is handed out carelessly by some irresponsible rock-quarry operators.
I brought this matter to the attention of the government during the winter. Are there any general restrictions in the bill? I am not a lawyer, and perhaps I am not qualified to interpret the bill fully, but does it contain any restrictive provisions which would bring pressure to bear upon the provinces, in the event of the use of explosives being under their jurisdiction? This is a matter which will have to be watched carefully, especially in rock quarries.

Section 4 (1) (c) states that regulations can be made for regulating the sale, importation, packing and handling of explosives, and the transportation of explosives. But there should be concurrent legislation in the provinces dealing with the utilization of explosives, especially in mines, or in respect of anyone wishing to use them for

Explosives Act
logging or blasting purposes. They would have to have a licence under this measure, when it becomes law.
What happens if a province does not pass legislation?
I do not think there will be any doubt as to their passing it. All the provinces will have legislation concurrent with ours, because they are seized of the duty of protecting operations of this kind.

At the present time if one wants to obtain fifteen or twenty sticks of dynamite, complete with fuses and caps, he must have a permit. Is that under dominion or provincial jurisdiction? If it is under the dominion, does the minister intend to keep it up? I hope he does. I bought dynamite only a month ago, but before doing so I had to get permission from the police, and to tell them what I wanted it for.
Does the hon. member suggest that there should be a permit?
There is one at the present time. When I wanted to buy the dynamite before I had to go to the Department of Munitions and Supply. Now I need only go to the local chief of police?
Yes.
And is that under dominion or provincial jurisdiction?
Dominion.
Does the government intend to continue this procedure?
We have the right to do it.
Do you not think you should?
You suggest that we should exercise that right?
I suggest to keep it on.

As I mentioned before, exception was taken, especially by farmers who would be going to a country store and who *would "have to get a permit signed by the magistrate or justice of the peace or mayor of the town. They complained bitterly about that inconvenience. We have the power to do it by regulation, and it is a matter that will receive most serious consideration when the regulations are being set up.

Before the war there used to be twenty, thirty or perhaps forty stores in my district which sold dynamite, caps and fuses at any time to those who wanted them. At the present time there are only about two
places, the quarry at Marmora and the board of works in Peterborough. Stores do not carry dynamite because they must keep it away from the store building and that costs money.

The minister has laid his finger upon the exact situation. The federal government has the power to restrict this thing, but from what he said I gathered that he was not inclined to take any steps in that direction. There may have been some complaints from farmers who wanted to blow up some stumps or something, but I would point out that in certain sections of this country there are men who are dangerous and who should be dealt with by the federal authorities. The damage that might be created by these men more than outweighs any inconvenience that might be caused to some farmers. I join with the hon. member for Peterborough West who states that this is most important. There are men of a type who are hardly safe to have in our communities and they should not be allowed to get explosives, particularly dynamite, with ease. Improper use might be made of it. There are sections of the country where the subversive element is certainly not growing any weaker. I think some hon. members have seen the development of certain activities and I plead with the minister to keep a close watch over this situation. If there is federal jurisdiction, I urge him to use it and not consider just the complaints of a farmer or two, even though they are bitter. With all due respect for what the minister says, I submit that this is flirting with something that might prove very damaging.
Flirting with dynamite.
It is flirting with dynamite, as the hon. member says. I urge the minister to retain the restrictions and not allow this to become the free and easy matter that it was before the war.

I was discussing that very point this morning and, as the hon. member has said, I am aware of the dangers that might be incurred. I assure him that I will give the matter the consideration it deserves.

While the minister is giving this matter consideration, I should like to raise something else for his consideration and the consideration of the hon. gentlemen who have just spoken. Do they suppose for one minute that there are not in the city of Toronto and in the government of Ontario men who are just as desirous of seeing public safety cared for as anyone in Ottawa?
Mr. . FRASER: Perhaps more so at the present time.
Explosives Act

Do they imagine that the city of Toronto is not as able to pass bylaws governing the sale of these dangerous explosives as is Ottawa? Do they imagine that the city of Toronto officials are not capable of doing this? There is a tendency, altogether too strong, to centralize power. That is not good. When the hon. member for Davenport read the account of this 'serious accident in Toronto it was well that he read also the statement that the city officials had taken action. Those officials do not need Ottawa to pass laws. They are just as much interested in the welfare of humanity as ever we can be. The fathers of confederation placed power in their hands and responsibilities on their shoulders for doing that very thing. I just wish to raise that for the consideration of the hon. member.
I consider the minister very wise to have been circumspect in connection with this matter and for having wondered whether or not it was necessary for Ottawa to do all the governing in Canada with respect to explosives. Let us not forget that the farther you get your government away from the people, the more you destroy democracy. The hon. member pointed out that matters were free and easy before the war. Did he hear of any serious accidents like that one in Toronto?
Yes, I have heard of them.

I am just wondering if we shall not hear of serious accidents after this legislation has been made as iron-clad as it is possible to make it. That accident was not caused by the fact that there was no iron-clad act in Ottawa; it was simply due to the human elements that enter into all relations. It has been my experience that where an accident of that sort takes place the local authorities are quite capable of adopting measures to deal with all such occurrences and to make provision against their recurrence.
Let us be careful about centralization. It is an easy matter to centralize power but it is very difficult to decentralize it and get it back into the hands of the people. All through the thousand years or more of our history we have been struggling to keep our power decentralized. Let us not in a period of hysteria brought on by a terrible war and rumours of communism and other dire threats forget the poise, balance and judgment which we inherited from our fathers who have gone before us.

I am not going to talk for a thousand years or anything of that kind; I simply want to point out that the provinces

have not the right to deal with this problem. Even if they had, anyone living on the border between two provinces could simply go into the other province. A man in Ontario could cross over into Quebec, purchase dynamite, and bring it back into Ontario. There is nothing to stop that. The dominion government have the right, and they are using that right, to regulate this matter. I am simply asking that there be some system of permits. If the dominion government is not going to do it, the provinces should. Perhaps the hon. member has tried to spank me, but I do not stay spanked very long.

If I were going to spank the hon. member I would spank him so that he would stay spanked. I was not criticizing particularly what the hon. member had to say; I was merely pointing out the danger of the tendency to centralization that is evident in the world to-day. There is not only centralization of power in Ottawa; it is going on to centralization in Geneva or Timbuktu where the people cannot possibly get at it.
This is an important point. I am not pronouncing whether the province has authority to deal with explosives or not, but obviously from what the hon. member for Davenport read, the city of Toronto considered that it had power to deal with the matter.
That was fireworks.
They are a form of explosives.
They have not been dealt with.

Then let them be dealt with. I am sure that they will be dealt with in Toronto and in other cities of Ontario and in other parts of Canada. But this parliament need not undertake to do everything for all the governments in Canada, for there are intelligent men in other government bodies.
We acknowledge that.

I was not in the chamber when the minister made his statement on the bill. I understand that it comes from the other house and that, therefore, there will not be a disposition to take as much time on it here as we otherwise would. Did the minister explain to the house the work which was put in on this bill in the other place? Did it receive mature consideration there? If the minister has already covered that point, perhaps he would restate it.

The bill was introduced in the other chamber, with a short explanation on

Explosives Act
the first reading and a discussion on the second reading, and then almost a whole afternoon was spent in considering the different sections of the bill. The result of this study is the bill now before us.
Where was the bill prepared? Is it a government measure?
Yes; it was prepared by the Department of Justice.

How many inspectors are employed under the act at the present time, and what does it cost in the course of a year to administer the act? I have the estimates for 1947 but I cannot find any item covering inspectors.

It is under Mines and
Geology.	,
Mr. HAZEI^: Yes, I see now that there is an item of $29,500. How many inspectors and sub-inspectors are working under the act at the present time?

We have a chief inspector, two inspectors and one chemist in the permanent establishment; and the clerical permanent staff includes one grade IV clerk, one grade II clerk, one stenographer grade II and one typist grade II. The temporary establishment includes three inspectors and a clerical staff consisting of two grade III clerks, three grade II clerks, three grade II stenographers, four grade II typists and one grade I-A typist. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police also serves voluntarily in connection with this work extensively throughout the dominion.
I see by the details that there is one chief inspector, and two inspectors of explosives.
We have a chief inspector, two inspectors and one chemist in the permanent establishment.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Explosives to which act applies.

May we take up on this section the question I raised as to whether it is quite clear that the crown company, Canadian Arsenals Limited, will by this measure be under the inspection, indeed the jurisdiction, of the Minister of Mines and Resources?
The bill when it comes into force will apply to all crown companies not under the control of the Department of National Defence, which will be subject to inspection under this measure.

So that the situation will be entirely altered in the future. In the past, before the war, the dominion arsenal was under the control of the Minister of National Defence, and inspection took place within it only by his authority. Canadian Arsenals Limited, which will be very much larger in scope than the dominion arsenal, will by this measure be under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Mines and Resources, so far as the inspection of the arsenal is concerned?

Section 3 says:
This act shall apply to the possession, storing, sale or offering for sale, making, manufacture or importation of explosives by or on behalf of His Majesty in right of Canada or any province except explosives under the direction or control of the Minister of National Defence.
The exception there is "explosives under the direction of the Minister of National Defence." I presume, therefore, that inspection of the arsenal would be under the direction of the Minister of National Defence if it is under his control.

This section applies to the possession, storing, sale or offering for sale, making, manufacture or importation of explosives. But there is another factor, and that is the disposal of explosives. Why should this measure not apply also to the disposal of explosives? There are at the present time, I believe, a good many surplus explosives in this country. Should not control over them be in the minister's hands just as much as control over the possession, storing, sale or offering for sale, making or manufacturing of explosives?
I do not want at the present time to go into details of the case I have in mind, but the disposal of explosives should be very carefully handled in order to prevent injury to civilians. Although I have not had an opportunity of giving this bill any particular study, it seems to me that the disposal of surplus explosives might very well be included in the measure. Is there any reason why the disposal of surplus explosives should not come under this bill? Why should not that be inserted in section 3?

I would take it that "possession, storing, sale or offering for sale" would cover the point the hon. gentleman raises, because that is the only way in which explosives can be disposed of except by destruction. If it were deteriorating and a danger to the community, there is power taken later in the bill to deal with such conditions. That, it seems to me, would cover the point raised by the hon. member-"sale or offering for sale".
Explosives Act

I am not referring to explosives which are sold or offered for sale; I refer to explosives which are being disposed of as surplus by the government. There are in this country to-day explosives which will be disposed of as surplus; there are explosives which have been disposed of as surplus, and in some instances, through negligence on somebody's'part, they have caused injury to Canadian citizens for which the government does not want to assume responsibility. As I say, I am not as familiar as the minister is with this bill, but it might be well if the "disposal" of these surplus munitions and explosives were included in this bill, in the interests of the citizens of this country.

Of course the hon. member will realize that under this bill there is power taken to make regulations which will cover anything dealing with the disposal of surplus such as the hon. member speaks of. What he is referring to is equipment and surplus munitions, and explosives which are unused and not likely to be used and therefore might be declared surplus. These go to the War Assets Corporation, which as a corporation would be subject to the provisions of this bill in the same way as anybody else would be. However, we might come to this later when we are dealing with the appropriate section.

I thought it would come under section 3, although I may be wrong; as I say, I do not profess to be familiar with this bill. The minister said that he would further consider section 2, paragraph (c). I wonder if it might not be advisable to give some consideration to the point I have raised concerning section 3, as to the disposal of surplus explosives. The question is this: should the word "disposal" be included in that section?

Would the minister be disposed, if to do so would not infringe upon provincial authority, to have someone in his department inquire into the matter which I brought up, namely as to how that merchant obtained possession for sale of high explosive rockets to children?
Power is taken under this bill to cause inquiry to be made into any accident of the nature spoken of.
Does the minister think this measure should not apply' to the disposal of surplus munitions and surplus explosives? I think I am entitled to an answer to that question.

The reason this section was put into the bill was in the light of the case of King versus LeBlanc, of which the hon.

member may have a more intimate knowledge than I, a case decided by Chief Justice Hazen in the Supreme Court of New Brunswick. The defendant was charged with negligence in the operation of explosives, and on appeal before the chief justice it was held that he was not within the purview of the provisions of the Explosives Act as it then stood. To correct that omission we have placed this section in the bill,' making all parties, even the crown and its employees, liable for any act of negligence under this measure. That is the whole reason why it was put in the bill. The sale, disposal and deterioration of * surpluses are covered in subsequent sections.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Regulations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Section carried.

Before this section 4 is carried I have a question to ask. I wish to compliment you, Mr. Chairman, on the able way you are putting the sections through; it shows great ability. I used to do the same thing myself when, in the old days, I was sitting where you are now. I did not allow anything to hang before the committee any longer than I could avoid. But now that I am in the opposition I have another duty to perform. As regards subsection 1, paragraph (d), "for holding inquiries into any accident caused by explosives," I would ask if the department would feel disposed to make an inquiry into the sale of rockets in Toronto, some ten days or two weeks ago, as the case may be, through which, a week ago last Sunday, a young man was killed on or near College and Clinton streets, Toronto, through the explosion of a rocket.

My officer informs me that the matter at the moment is in the hands of the municipal police, but he will take such steps *"as the hon. gentleman suggests, in conjunction with the municipal police, for the holding of an inquiry such as the hon. member suggests, to find out exactly what took place.
That is quite satisfactory. The matter would, I think, come under paragraph (h), enabling regulations to be made "for the safety of the public."
May I ask the minister if he held any inquiry into an accidental explosion at Lomeville, New Brunswick, in January of this year?
No; no inquiry was made.

Section agreed to.	[DOT]
Sections 5 and 6 agreed to.
On section 7-Certificate to store.

Explosives Act

Under this section would the department or someone authorized by the department be enabled to inquire whether such a store as must have sold these high explosive rockets was a fit place to store them?
Under this section a certificate will only be issued to any person permitting the storing for sale of explosives on such premises and in such quantity as the minister may determine.
That would apply to a retail store, would it not?

These would be what we call registered premises, and the certificate would have to be issued by the minister, who would have to be satisfied as to the suitability of the premises and also as to the quantity which might be allowed to.be stored in that store.

Section agreed to.
Sections 8 to 18 inclusive agreed to.
On section 19-Minister may direct inquiry.
In the event of an accident such as that which caused the recent lamentable death of a young man in Toronto, this section could be put into operation?
Yes.

Section agreed to.
Sections 20 to 28 inclusive agreed to.
On section 29-Repeal.
Will the minister tell me the sections of the bill that have to do with the disposal of explosives? He said that as we went through the bill we would come to those sections.

The hon. member will find that the regulations under section 4 are extensive. I cannot imagine anything that has not been included in them. I have gone over them carefully with the officers, and they assure me that the regulations provide all the power necessary for governing the sale of explosives, the taking of them, the procedure to be followed, the construction and management of premises, the safety of the public, and so forth. The sale and disposal of explosives would be covered by the regulations. The bill provides for forfeiture, where officers have the power of inspection and can enter premises. Under section 18 the officers can go into premises and take samples of explosives, open and examine them and may require the owners to give evidence with respect to
such samples, and later, on conviction, the explosives can be forfeited by the crown and destroyed or sold in the discretion of the crown. The hon. gentleman is worried about the word "disposal" and the word "sale".
Not so much "sale" as "disposal".
I think the word "sale1' will cover exactly what he has in mind. Sale will include disposal, and the word "disposal" will not add to the strength of it.
If a department of government decides to dispose of surplus explosives, I do not think that by any stretch of the imagination that can be called a sale. It should come under this measure.
By giving it away or destroying it?
Not by giving it away but by destroying it-disposing of it in the sense of destroying it so that it will not cause injury to anyone.

Under section 27, where a conviction is obtained, the explosives are forfeit to the crown and may be destroyed or otherwise disposed of, as may be thought fit. I think it covers handling from first to last; the officers assure me that the matter has been fully considered and they are quite satisfied.
Section 27 does not cover the case I have in mind. I do not want to labour the matter but I submit that it is not covered in the bill.
What would happen to surplus bombs in the hands of War Assets Corporation?
They are subject to the jurisdiction of this measure if there is any danger to the public in storage or handling.

This matter was discussed briefly in the house either on a question or in some other way during the last session, or perhaps during this session. Certain explosives were disposed of by the Royal Canadian Air Force by being dumped into the ocean, but they were not dumped far enough out, so that when the tide went out some youngsters went out and picked up some of the explosives. Some of the children were injured.

Section agreed to.
Section 1 agreed to.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
National Parks

After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section 2-Definitions.

The hon. member for Lake Centre asked: Is it the opinion of the law officers of the crown that section 2 (c) and section 4 would cover a case such as that referred to by the hon. member for Davenport? During the recess this point was discussed with the officers of the justice department, as well as the deputy minister, who expressed the opinion that the bill as drafted would include and cover the kind of explosive used in the instance referred to by the hon. member for Davenport. The technical officers of the department were also consulted, and they are satisfied that this provision fully covers the case mentioned by the hon. gentleman. The hon. member for Lake Centre stated that if the Department of Justice approved it,-he was satisfied.

Section agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed. NATIONAL PARKS

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: ADJUSTMENT OP BOUNDARIES IN RESPECT OP CERTAIN SMALL AREAS
speechtext:
When this bill was before the committee of the whole previously all the sections were carried, and the committee was considering the title.
On the title.

maintopic: ADJUSTMENT OP BOUNDARIES IN RESPECT OP CERTAIN SMALL AREAS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Dauphin, the hon. member for Calgary West and I think the hon. member for Mackenzie asked questions with regard to the purchase of additional land for the Banff national park. The small parcels of land being added comprise (a) approximately 210 acres at the eastern gateway. This was transferred to the dominion by the province by P.C. 714-333 dated September 12, 1933. The original order in council was registered in the south Alberta land titles office at Calgary. Duplicate certificates of title Nos. 47X181 and 47X182 were received covering the parcels of land in question. These were dated October 31, 1933. I might say that one duplicate certificate of title covered those parts of the north half of section 13 and the northeast quarter of section 14, township 25, range 11, west of the 5th meridian,

.lying southeast of the then park boundary. The other covered the portion of the Banff-Calgary road lying within the above area.
(b) The second area in question comprises one-sixth of a square mile in the Spray river valley. speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: PROVISION FOR MORE EFFECTIVE CONTROL-STRINGENT REGULATION IN SUPPLY OF MORPHINE AND OPIUM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill comes from the senate. When it was in the other place it was referred to the standing committee on health and welfare, -where it received consideration.
Sections 1, 2 and 7 of the bill make a simple change in the name of the department, to conform to the creation of the Department of Health and Welfare, which took place as of October 13, 1944.
Section 3 replaces the word "distributes" by the word "administers", and I believe the explanatory note covers the point sufficiently.
Sections 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9 carry into the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act of 1929 provisions which were made effective by P.C. 4769 of June 10, 1943, P.C. 6227 of August 8, 1944, and P.C. 7096 of November 27, 1945. The effect of these is to make the control of narcotics more effective in Canada and also to carry into our peace-time legislation provisions found necessary and desirable during the war. We explain these by saying that during the war the supply situation in connection with
Narcotic Drug Act

narcotics presented many difficulties and, in order to conserve our supplies, which were short, and to secure more effective control, it became desirable to make changes in the laws by orders in council under the War Measures Act.
The changes which were made were to make the supply of drugs as defined in the act subject to prescription, and the other controls exercised under section 5 of the act effective without the same exceptions there had been been under section 8. Under section 8 of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, 1929, there was an exception under which it was possible for retail druggists to distribute small quantities of drugs, including morphine and opium, without prescription. During the war that exception was eliminated. The only relaxation to that exception since the war is that the only quantities of drugs which can be distributed without prescription are drugs containing small quantities of codeine.
That exception has been earned into effect in the bill. Consequently the bill substantially carries into effect the war-time provisions so as to effect a more stringent regulation in the supply of drugs such as morphine and opium. The changes are largely technical. They were made after consultation with the Dominion Council of Health and the advisory committee of the Canadian Medical association, both of which recommended them to the department. The only suggestion that we went too far came from one provincial medical association. We answered them, and since then we have received no word that anyone thought we were not doing 'the right thing.

Now it happens that section 4, paragraph (f) also contains this same word "distributes"; the language is almost the same as that of paragraph (e). I wonder if it was by intent that section 4, paragraph (f) is not to be amended in like manner as section 4, paragraph (e). Section 4, paragraph (e) reads:
Every person who
(e)	unlawfully sells, gives away or distributes any drug to any minor . . .
Paragraph (f) reads:
(f)	manufactures, sells, gives away or distributes any drug . . .
And so on. We have the word "distributes" in (f) as well as in (e). We have amended it in (e) only to substitute the word "administers" for "distributes". Would the minister indicate why we are not contemplating a similar amendment of section 4, subsection 1, paragraph (f).

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: PROVISION FOR MORE EFFECTIVE CONTROL-STRINGENT REGULATION IN SUPPLY OF MORPHINE AND OPIUM
speechtext:
The two clauses are designedly different. In the present act, section 4, subsection 1, paragraph (e) reads:
Every person who
(e) unlawfully sells, gives away or distributes any drug to any minor;
In the case of Rex versus Marino and Yipp, 56 Canadian Criminal Cases, page 139, the supreme court, speaking through Chief Justice Anglin, held that in order to constitute a "distribution" within the meaning of paragraph (f) it was necessary for more than one act to take place. There could not be a distribution within the meaning of the act unless there had been more than one delivery of a drug to the person who received it. When we considered the act in the light of war-time experience and in the light of that decision we considered it desirable to change the provision with regard to selling, giving away or distributing any drug to any minor so to make the offence one of "administering" drugs to any minor, because it was almost inconceivable that there should be a repeated delivery of drugs to a minor. We thought
the one administration of a drug to a minor was sufficient to constitute an offence, and a very serious offence too. This, therefore, led us to propose in this bill the substitution of the word "administers" for the word "distributes" in paragraph (e), but to leave the provision in paragraph (f) as it was.

speechtext: I follow the minister's explanation as to the change in section 4, subsection 1 (e); I think it is quite in line with the decision he refers to in Rex versus Marino and Yipp. I understand that decision was based on section 4, subsection 1 (e) not on section 4 subsection 1 (f). I am not quite clear yet, if I may say so, as to the reason why we are not making a corresponding change in section 4, subsection 1 (f). The language is the same in the two clauses. In paragraph (e) it is "sells, gives away or distributes"; in paragraph (f) it is "manufactures, sells, gives away or distributes" any drug.

The offence which was involved in the case of Rex versus Marino and Yipp was an offence charged under paragraph (f) of subsection 1 of section 4, and the language of (f) is quite suitable for an offence charged in connection with the distribution of drugs to someone other than a minor. Section 4, subsection 1 (f) reads:
Every person who manufactures, sells, gives away, delivers or distributes or makes any offer in respect of any drug or any substance . . .
And so on. That seems to be quite suitable language with respect to an offence in connection with delivery and so on to an adult, but in order to strengthen the law governing delivery of any drug to a minor we propose to substitute the word "administers" for the word "distributes" in (e).

maintopic: PROVISION FOR MORE EFFECTIVE CONTROL-STRINGENT REGULATION IN SUPPLY OF MORPHINE AND OPIUM
speechtext: Does not the minister consider it proper to insert the word "administers" in section 4, 1 (f) ? Then we should have it both ways, covering the manufacture, sale, giving away, administration or distribution, and we should strengthen the section greatly. Would it not be wise to insert the word "administers" after the words "gives away"?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: PROVISION FOR MORE EFFECTIVE CONTROL-STRINGENT REGULATION IN SUPPLY OF MORPHINE AND OPIUM
speechtext:
The officer of the department charged with the administration of the act says that there has never been a case in which the necessity for such a change has arisen, and we, I understand, have had cases in which we found it difficult, if not impossible,-to prove an offence under section 4, (1) (e) with regard to a minor because of lack of the language I suggest should be adopted. We have not had any such case under 4, (1) (ff).

Air Force Act-Cadet Squadrons

speechtext: When the minister refers to drugs he means narcotics?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: PROVISION FOR MORE EFFECTIVE CONTROL-STRINGENT REGULATION IN SUPPLY OF MORPHINE AND OPIUM
speechtext:
Yes. The Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, 1929, as amended in 1932, defines "drugs" as follows, in Section 2 (d):
"Drug" means and includes any substance, mentioned in the schedule to this act whether or not the same be produced in whole or in part by a synthetic process, and whether it be alone or in conjunction with any other substance mentioned in the schedule to this act, or which may be added to such schedule under the authority of this act.
Then we have the schedule which is revised under this bill and which is tied in to the act, and it defines drugs as narcotics, opium, coca leaf, and so on.
