Hon. COLIN GIBSON (Minister of National Defence for Air) moved the second reading of bill No. 57, to amend the Royal Canadian Air Force Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.
Will the minister give a general statement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The purpose of the bill is to make provision under the Royal Canadian Air Force Act for the continuation of the Royal Canadian Air Force cadet squadrons which were first formed during the war in 1940 by order in council under the War Measures Act. It now becomes necessary, if they are to be continued, to make provision for them under the act.
In this connection the committee will be interested to know that in the short space of six years during which they have been operating the air cadets have built up an excellent reputation for themselves. The air cadet squadrons are operated under the control and jurisdiction of the air cadet league, and a great deal of credit is owing to the members of the air cadet league, the provincial committees, and the members in the various municipalities throughout Canada who have sponsored the air cadet squadrons. They have raised funds provincially and locally to provide for these squadrons, and the success of the air cadet movement is due largely to the tremendous amount of work done by members of the air cadet league in sponsoring and supporting the various air cadet squadrons.
During the war we had 400 squadrons in operation in Canada. At present there are 289 squadrons active with an enrolment of something over 23,000 air cadets. It is now proposed to provide for them so that we shall continue to have the air cadets as part of the cadet system of the country, very much as the army cadets have been provided for heretofore under the terms of the Militia Act.

Do I understand from the minister that the air cadet corps operates directly under the Royal Canadian Air Force and that, while the air cadet league is a useful help and auxiliary to it, it is not necessary for the league to exist in order that the cause should succeed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: No; it is almost the opposite. The air cadet league is responsible for these cadet squadrons, but the bill before the committee permits the Royal Canadian Air Force to make provision for training and a certain amount of financial assistance is required to operate these squadrons. The air cadet league itself also raises money from the public to provide for some of the expenses of maintaining these squadrons. No squadrons can become air cadet squadrons unless they have been approved by the Minister of National Defence for Air. Also a syllabus of training is drawn up by the Department of National Defence for Air. There is the closest liaison between the air department and the air cadet league, and, when any matters arise that need adjustment they are settled by consultation between the department and the league.

Mr. Chairman, as one who has had something to do with the air cadet movement in Canada I should like to say that I am heartily in support of this bill which carries into the peace a movement which was efficient, which gave young men good training and which imbued them with the ideals of the service. In my opinion there are many who should be thanked for their splendid services in building up this great corps. There are the directors of the air cadet league and the provincial committees, with particular reference to the provinces of Ontario and British Columbia, and I am sure the government will be glad to know that the government of Ontario have made provision for the continuation of this splendid service through the appointment of Air Commodore O'Brien, an ex-R.C.A.F. auxiliary officer, who gave service overseas in this war and who now continues to serve the air force through his connection with the Ontario government. In addition, there are many schools, many schoolteachers, many air cadet officers and the sponsors, whom
fMr. Claxton.]

Air Force Act-Cadet Squadrons
the minister has already mentioned in connection with the local committees. Then there are so many others of the general public who gave generously of their finances, their time and their personal efforts to this corps. I would not like to overlook at this time the many men in the permanent establishment of the R.C.A.F., and those who served with it in war time, who have been unsparing in their time and trouble. I have in mind one particular case; that is, the men in the training branch of the Royal Canadian Air Force, who have done a splendid job in preparing a completely new syllabus of instruction for the air cadets.
Last year at this time I had the honour of inspecting three air cadet squadrons in the city of Toronto. That took place during the election, from which I was glad to take a little time, and I was indeed impressed with the efficiency and discipline of these young men. At this time I should like to say I feel that the grants of money which will be given by the country to these air cadet squadrons will be repaid tenfold in citizenship in the years to come. I hope there will never be any argument or quibbling in this house over, these grants, particularly at a time like this when we all see the danger of juvenile delinquency which was exemplified in an unfortunate case only the other day, when four young men were condemned to prison for the shooting of a man in the city of Toronto. I feel that any money we can put into such things as the air cadet movement will be for the good of the country and to our own advantage in time to come.

If I understood the minister aright, there is to be a diminution in the number of squadrons from 400 to something like 289. Would the minister give us the reason for this reduction? My experience in an institution with which I had something to do was that when the chance of becoming airmen disappeared, a good deal of enthusiasm for the air cadet corps also disappeared. When the war was practically won and the air force gave notice that no more of these boys would be accepted into the regular force, we noticed a tremendous lessening of enthusiasm. I was wondering to what extent that lack of enthusiasm exists in the squadrons remaining, and to what extent air cadet training may be in a sense compulsory in certain of the schools or institutions which still carry it on.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
During the war it was considered advisable to start air cadet squadrons in many centres throughout Canada. Experience has shown, however, that while many squadrons have done well, others have not flourished, and to keep up
the standard that the air force wishes to maintain throughout the country it is considered better to have fewer and better squadrons rather than to try to have a large number of squadrons, many of which would be inefficient. At the same time, as hon. members know, the air force has been cut down from a peak of over 200,000 to something over 16,000. Too many air cadets would mean that only a very 'small percentage could be absorbed into the permanent and auxiliary air force. We look forward to having many boys who have trained in the air cadet squadrons come into the permanent and auxiliary forces and I am glad to say that, of the. new recruits who have enlisted recently, I am informed that approximately one-third received their early training in the air cadet squadrons. So that we prefer to have a smaller number of squadrons, and have them all good. As hon. members will see in the bill, the age limit is from fifteen to eighteen, which provides for boys taking a fairly advanced course which has been laid out for them. When they have finished that course they will then be in line to go into either the regular air force or one of the auxiliary squadrons.
Does the service contemplate assisting the air cadets with actual air instruction at summer camps, or anything of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I do not want to make any definite commitment on that yet, because the matter is still receiving consideration by the air force and the air cadet league. It is hoped, however, that a certain number of the top-notch cadets, as a sort of prize, will be permitted to obtain some instruction in actual flying. But while cadets at summer camps are given familiarization flights-that is, they are taken up in the air-that does not mean they are all taught to handle a plane. It is hoped, however, that a few of them will be able to secure that instruction.

Do the minister's remarks
include gliding instruction as well?
Mr, GIBSON (Hamilton West): It is a little too early to say what steps will be taken in regard to gliding. I know that subject has been receiving careful consideration by the air cadet league, and quite a long report has been put in by the subcommittee which has been looking into the matter.

I believe the minister is to be commended for putting these air cadets on a solid footing. I well remember that after the last war anything pertaining to military

Air Force Act-Cadet Squadrons
training was tabooed by schoolboards, students in universities and so on, as teaching war. I do not know how a group of boys could be better trained than in an air cadet squadron. We have one at the head of the lakes, and we are extremely proud of it. If you keep a boy busy with good things the police will not even know that he exists. Putting this force on a permanent basis, is, I think, a good thing; and while they are not liable to service in an emergency that does not mean they are barred. As I look at it, that just means they are not compelled to serve. I heartily commend the minister for having taken this step.

Would the minister care to indicate whether any preference is given at the present time to air cadets who would like to enlist in the Royal Canadian Air Force? According to a recent newspaper item, I believe there is some little difficulty in getting men for groundcrews. I do not know how accurate that statement is, but the minister might indicate whether or not the boys who graduate from the courses in our high schools along air cadet lines receive preference over other boys who had no such training.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I can say that the training they received has made them more valuable than those who have not had the training. As I said, approximately a third of those who have already enlisted are boys who have had senior air cadet training in air cadet squadrons.

In the smaller towns of around 6,000 population, such as the one from which I come, air cadet corps were sponsored during the war. Also in those towns are found sea cadet and army cadet corps. They were operating at sixes, there not being enough to make one good corps in any one of them.
To-day the situation is the same. We have the air cadet corps and the army cadet corps, and it is now being decided whether the air cadet corps will carry on. Does the minister offer any solution of that problem, or will they be formed only in the larger centres?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The plan of the air cadets league is to allocate squadrons, having a certain quota for each province. I am glad that the question in connection with the multiplicity of squadrons has been mentioned. That is a condition which grew up out of the war. We have a joint interdepartmental committee on cadets, including army, navy and air. I am anxious to have that committee work out many details which will arise, such as the pay which should be

given to the various units, the regulations concerning uniforms, instructors and the like, so that the support which the government provides for the various cadet corps will be as uniform as possible throughout the three services. When that committee meets questions such as those respecting three squadrons in one small community could foe ironed out, with a view to having only one squadron instead of three allocated to that community.

Does the minister not believe some inducement should be held out to the boys who are taking air cadet training? That is one of the reasons I asked whether they received preference over other boys who might wish to join the regular Royal Canadian Air Force. I believe this is an important point.
I was air cadet liaison officer for some time in the air force. The boys asked time and again whether or not they would get preference, but I could not hold out any hope. If some inducement were given them they would go after the training much more wholeheartedly.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
Toward the end of the war the air force stopped recruiting, and it was most discouraging for air cadets who had joined the cadet squadrons, hoping thereby to get into the air force, to find that all entry into that force was closed off because of a cessation of recruiting.
That condition, of course, does not exist to-day. Any air cadet who is fit and efficient -certainly at the present time, while recruiting is going on-can count upon his being accepted. I am sure he would be accepted, so long as he is physically and mentally fit for enlistment.

I assure the minister I am in favour of his bill, but there is one point I should like to draw to his attention. I feel that air cadet training officers are being penalized. I know of one air cadet training officer who during 1945 attended a two weeks' course in the month of March, and then in the summer attended twelve days at camp with the boys. On both occasions he received pay and allowances but, as hon. members know, those payments do not compensate one for out-of-pocket expenses. Any cadet training officer has his hand continually in his pocket for this, that and the other thing. However, this officer, after having attended the course and camp, and having received pay and allowances, found, when he - went to pay his income tax, that the pay and allow- ' ances received placed him in a higher category', with the result that he had to pay a penalty of $50. This was all the thanks he

Air Force Act-Cadet Squadrons
got for having performed that very fine work in the cadet corps. Surely this is a matter which should be considered carefully.

The work accomplished for the youth of our country by the army, naval and air cadet corps is vital. In one of the towns of my constituency we have a naval cadet corps. The boys in that corps are definitely being kept off the streets. The reduction in our juvenile delinquency is marked, owing to the activity of the navy league in that community. But they are trying to carry on in an old Y.M.C.A. building.
In the past, governments have been prone to neglect the erection of armouries for army personnel in communities. In our community the volunteers meet once a week, and the officers meet three times in their mess, possibly enjos'ing a drink. But the building in which they meet looks like a gaol. It is an eyesore, and quite unfit for the purpose to which it is being put. It contains no swimming pool, no gymnasium, or anything of the kind.
I suggest that the Minister of National Defence for Air, in conjunction with the minister for the army and naval services, consider seriously aiding communities in the erection of armouries, or buildings adequate to house these military units. There should be gymnasiums and swimming pools where both boys and girls in the community could assemble on different nights. Let them develop their bodies and they will develop their minds. Never has a greater development of youth been more necessary in Canada, after the trials and tribulations of the war, after watching the suffering of the older people and watching the struggles through which they have gone.
I suggest that the minister and his colleague should get into communication with the various communities. I can assure him that the town in my community would be willing to contribute any reasonable amount, in conjunction with the government, for the erection of such a building, where youth could assemble and keep off the streets.
The improvement brought about by the activities of the navy league in our community is striking. I saw the boys who had been carrying out their training. Last week, when a presentation of the bell from the corvette Collingwood was made, I saw the boys who have been carrying out this training. Their discipline was perfect, every movement the movement of veterans. But those chaps had learned those drills in a room only twenty feet by thirty-five feet.
There is no accommodation in the town for the young girls. If the minister were to train a cadet corps in our community, I am wondering where they would assemble. They are barred from the collegiate and the schools. The playgrounds are quite inadequate and not fit for the children to play on.
It behooves the government to go into the matter carefully with all communities across the country so as to arrive at something which will benefit our boys and girls, and give them what they need.

I do not know to what minister I should direct the suggestion I have in mind in'connection with Boy Scout work and its association with the air cadets. As I pointed out a moment ago, we find that Boy Scouts make the most apt air cadets of all. They have had good training in citizenship and physical culture, and I think some cognizance should be taken by the government of the activities of this organization. I understand that at the present time it receives an appropriation of $5,000 for the whole dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to the National Physical Fitness Act?
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The total grant is $250,000 by the dominion government, on a fifty-fifty basis with the provinces. Up to the present time seven out of nine provinces are taking part.	[DOT]
Is that the appropriation for Boy Scout work?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For youth organizations of all kinds throughout Canada.
Is that one of the organizations you have referred to? I understood the appropriation was S5,000 and I do not think it is enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The grant to the Boy Scouts is $9,000.
. Mr. WEBB: I am fully in accord with the principles of this bill, but I should like to clear up the matter which was brought up by the hon. member for Durham. We have the army cadets, the navy cadets and the air cadets, and in smaller communities there is a possibility of friction, of one-organization taking members from the other. Whose responsibility is it to settle a matter of this kind when there are not enough boys to carry on the three services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
It would come under the air cadet league itself, and also the navy league. What happens in a great many centres is that some organization such as the Lions club, the Rotary club or some other

Air Force * Act-Cadet Squadrons
club sponsors a squadron. If they should be sucessful in raising a good squadron of approximately fifty boys it would be continued. If there were two or three cadet units in a community, all of which were under strength and competing with each other, I think the authorities would get together and decide which would be continued. Neither the navy league nor the air cadet league nor the army want to have inefficient squadrons that are under strength and not pulling their own weight.
As I understand it, a branch of the sea cadets cannot be set up in a small community until it has the sanction of the navy league headquarters in Ottawa.

I am in support of the bill, but for different reasons from those of most people. I am heartily in favour of it because of the discipline upon our youth which measures such as this impose. Many people blame the delinquency of our youth upon conditions of home life, and many other excuses are made. I have an idea that there are some bad boys, and this was exemplified in Toronto the other day when four boys ranging from fifteen to twenty-one years of age went out and murdered an old chap who had built himself a little business. They were found guilty of manslaughter and two of them were sentenced to gaol for fifteen yearn, the other two receiving a sentence of twenty years each. The excuse for this was bad home conditions and no opportunity for employment. Everybody knows that since the war started six years ago there has been a shortage of man-power and there is no reason why anyone should not find employment. An old fellow by the name of Tobias is dead and his murderers are jitter-bugging in Toronto gaol and laughing at the administration of justice because the sob-sisters have finally accomplished their purposes.
Is the number of corps and the number of personnel that can be enlisted limited?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: We have had discussions with, the air cadet league and they have come to the conclusion that they should endeavour to maintain approximately 200 squadrons w'ith a personnel of 15,000 all told. This would mean the squadrons would range from fifty up.
May I ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs if I am correct in understanding that we are spending $9,000 on the Boy Scouts this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was the Minister of Finance who said that. The grant for the Boy Scouts for many years has been $9,000, and it is $9,000 this year.

When I was advocating the erection of a building to accommodate the youth of our country I had in mind the burden that might be imposed upon our taxpayers. I am now told that we grant $9,000 to the Boy Scouts organization to build up our youth. I find that this government is spending $25,000 to distribute a French and English dictionary to the members of parliament of this country. I think the government had better stop that and do a little more for the Boy Scouts.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to contradict my hon. friend, but I claim that the federal government's responsibility is much more involved in the field of education of our people for the purpose of ensuring a better comprehension of the rights of the minority, by some, and the rights of the majority, by others, than in a field which is the exclusive responsibility of the provincial governments. (Text):
If my hon. friend does not understand me it proves that we need to spend $25,000 for dictionaries, and perhaps that is not enough.
Mr. Chairman

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The committee is considering bill No. 57, to amend the Royal Canadian Air Force Act. I would remind hon. members of the committee that when the house is in committee, according to standing order 58, subsection 2, all discussion must be strictly relevant to the matter under discussion.
No person could learn English or French from the dictionary to which I referred. It is a political dictionary.
Has the minister been able to secure from War Assets Corporation or from his department any equipment for the air cadets that would help to keep them interested in their work?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: The Royal Canadian Air Force supplies the air cadet squadrons with a great deal of, if not with all the equipment that they use in their instructional work, as wrell as the arms with which they are trained.
I am thinking of the aeroplane instruments, engines and one thing and another like that which they should have so that they can see what they will have to work with later on.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
These are not provided from War Assets but direct from the air force. Equipment required by the air

Air Force Act-Cadet Squadrons
cadets is supplied, if available, by the air force, which turns it over rather than declaring it surplus to War Assets.

What provision is being made to assist in air force training in the schools? There is a lot of equipment available that would be acceptable to the schools. What is the government's policy as to assisting in that work?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The provision of equipment to technical schools is an entirely different matter. This bill is dealing only with the formation of air cadet corps, and it does not cover the supplying of equipment to educational institutions.
Mr. LOCKHART; Some of the schools have in mind that their educational courses will lead to air cadet work, hoping that the boys will eventually become air-minded. They will at least have the fundamentals, and it is expected that many of the boys will want to go into the air cadets. I have heard that thought expressed several times.

The minister has said that at present the government envisage a maximum of 15,000 air cadets. Will they be evenly distributed across the country? The province of Quebec had some most efficient corps in the war, ably trained, and there were also some in the maritimes, Ontario, the prairie provinces and British Columbia. I believe there are now more than 12,000 air cadets in Ontario alone, so that Ontario and British Columbia would absorb the whole quota which the minister mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: The air cadet squadrons will be distributed on the same basis as now through all the provinces. Prince Edward Island may have more squadrons. I think they have one-now, and that number will probably be increased. That is a matter which is being worked out with the air cadet league, but no definite decision has been reached.

The departments of education of the various provinces have to know how many corps they can put into the various schools. Every provincial department of education requires to know how many air cadets it can have and how many schools it can put them into, if the minister intends to have squadrons in the public schools.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
A great many squadrons will carry on as they have in the past. Some squadrons which have not been functioning up to the proper degree of efficiency may be disbanded. We had 400 squadrons at the peak during the war. A great many of them have folded up for one
reason or another. We have only 289 at the present time. Many of these squadrons had both senior and junior cadets. When you eliminate the juniors it does not leave enough seniors in some squadrons to make it worth while to carry on the squadrons with the few seniors available.

Is it necessary that these be designated as air force squadrons or air force cadets? I was interested in the suggestion made by several members that these various squadrons should be grouped together. There is no particular need, as far as I can see, to give specialized training to boys of that age either in air force, army or navy work. One solution of the problem suggested in the town I come from was that the only way a cadet force could be carried on was to put the three divisions together. We could have a cadet corps in connection with high school work and we need not give them particularly specialized training. In the event of war these boys would have had some military training and they could then join special branches. But for the purpose of that discipline which has been mentioned by hon. gentlemen to my right and for the purpose of promoting citizenship, or merely for the negative purpose of keeping the boys off the street, a combined corps is just as good, and it has not some of the objections which a military organization has in the minds of a good many people.

I wish to commend the minister for the idea of having a cadet corps, but I believe that this plan is not nearly comprehensive enough. I do not really see why it should be necessary to cut down the number of squadrons in order to improve their quality. I gathered from what the minister said that he would rather have a few squadrons and have them exceptionally good. I am not able to see why we should not have a large number of squadrons and have them all good. I believe the motivation must be at fault.
. The idea which seems to be in the minds of those who are organizing this cadet movement is that the boys shall be prepared to go into the permanent force. I do not believe that is the basis upon which we should proceed. There should be the ideal of being prepared. I do not wish to say any harsh thing, but it looks to me almost as though the minister's was a policy of defeatism. All we need to do is to get the hints that are dropped of the colossal and systematic preparations which are being made in a certain country to realize that if we should ever become involved with a nation like that one, no small air force will be in any way adequate to the

Air Force Act-Cadet Squadrons
situation. I believe that we should start right now to teach our boys and girls and our people throughout the country that we are living in the most dangerous time that has ever existed in the history of this nation or this race. All our boys and girls throughout our schools everywhere ought to be taught definitely that we have never yet acknowledged publicly in this country what are the causes of war. No one in this government since I have been here has ever breathed a word concerning the real causes of war, and no member of the opposition since I have been here has ever said a word concerning the real causes of war. The result is that people are being deluded into thinking that all we need to remove war is a sufficiently powerful united nations organization.	-
So long as the causes of war are not publicly acknowledged and so long as nothing is done to remove those causes of war, we are in danger of an outbreak of war any week from now on, and the people ought to know that. Every person in public life with responsibility ought to tell them that. If the boys and girls were told that in the schools and were given to understand that it is their duty to prepare for war if it comes, it seems to me that we would have a motivation which would encourage a very large percentage of our boys to enter training for the services. It ought to be made perfectly clear to them that the next war will be a war of instants, a war of minutes. There will not be any possibility of holding the foe back of any Maginot line or any other line or behind any ocean while we commence three or four years of preparation to make up for what we have lost. If we are not thoroughly prepared when the enemy strikes the next time, the first battle will be the last. Our boys ought to be taught that: they are the ones who are going to suffer; why should they not be told the truth? They ought to know also that the next war will be a global war; it will be global war from the very first move. Canada will be in the front line; Canada will be a theatre of actual conflict. That is the most certain conclusion that the ablest thinkers in military matters are able to arrive at to-day.
Why not tell the boys and girls about this? Why not say to them, "Boys, you cannot afford to be unprepared when the time of decision comes." Everyone in this country ought to be ready for immediate action until such time as the causes of war, the great, fundamental, economic, inevitable causes of war are discovered and provision is made for removing them.
So I think that for the minister to speak as modestly as he is doing, about an air force
[Mr. BlackmoreJ
of only 16,000, is for him to undershoot the mark a great deal. -I am convinced that the minister feels that way himself, and I would not be surprised if he had wondered whether the' house would accept favourably his offering even at this rate. Perhaps he is happily surprised to find that we are all with him. But what we are looking for is bold, aggressive, determined, adequate leadership to make this country ready to perform its part in whatever conflict may arise. That, I would say, is the main motivation which should be used for the boys, not the idea that when they are finished with the cadet training they should be able to go into the permanent force. That is not what they are going into it for, not by 'any manner of means. I believe that every school from coast to coast in this country should be making provision for the training of boys for the services into which they may have to go any day.
There is another basis of motivation about which I should like to have heard something but, as far as I know, the minister did not mention it. I wonder whether provision has been made for summer camps in the various provinces, so that cadet groups can go to those camps and spend a month or six weeks there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: Yes; it is planned that they will go to summer camps for two weeks.

That is a proper motivation, and the provision of proficiency cups and shields will give another incentive for the boys to go in and do their best. So that we ought to have no difficulty at all, I would suppose, in getting all the boys we can use, and we certainly ought not to have any difficulty in using all the boys that come forward. All the boys in the country should be welcomed and encouraged to be trained.
I was thinking, just before I commenced to speak, along these lines: if we are to have only 16,000 air cadets, or 16,000 in the permanent air force, is that somewhere near all we shall have in the naval force, and is that somewhere near all we are to have in the army? If that is so, obviously our permanent force is going to be far too small. I am not a specialist in this subject, but these are considerations which are passing through my mind. I wonder whether the minister is entirely wise in saying that he is thinking about cutting down the number of cadet groups, in order to raise the efficiency.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
There is no figure in the legislation. That is the basis we are working on with the air cadet league. They are prepared to sponsor that number of

Air Force Act-Cadet Squadrons
cadets at the present time, but there is no limitation on the number of air cadets that may be taken on by agreement between the league and the department. The suggestion that all cadets that are taken in are expected to go into the permanent force is, of course, not sound, in view of the fact that the cadets will only be in the air cadet corps for approximately three years each. That would be, with 15,000, five thousand coming out each year, and obviously the regular force could not absorb that number if they all wanted to enlist. But it is hoped that a large number will go into the auxiliary squadrons.

That is why I think that the more general approach as regards the air cadets in order to qualify for the air force is fallacious, that the boys should never be enrolled in the cadet corps with the idea that they are to qualify for the permanent air force.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I did not say they were enrolled for that purpose; I said it would give them perference for the air force if they wished to enlist.

I wonder if I have gathered this right. The impression I have is that the department is remaining more or less passive and in the background and is waiting for the air cadet league to take the initiative. That is, the air cadet league decides that it wants to have another cadet group; it asks the department for permission to have one, and the department gives its consent. Is that the general procedure?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: No; they are far more closely integrated than that, because, after all, the major expenditures on this whole air cadet movement are defrayed by the Department of National Defence for Air. Consequently the control is in the department, for it has to supply a considerable portion of the funds, a great part of the arms and equipment, and, to some extent, the clothing. So that there is close cooperation between the two. But certainly the matter of finance must always be considered in connection with authorizing unlimited numbers of squadrons.

There is no question that the matter of finance must be considered. I grant that; we are not doubting that for a minute. But if we were to plunge into war in six weeks' time we would forget finance immediately. That must impress on every hon.
member the fact that in the last analysis finance has to be the servant and not the master. What I would like the minister to make quite clear is, just what is the relation between the department and the air cadet league? Does the department organize the air cadet league? Does it motivate it? Does it initiate its action? How does the air cadet league come to take its part?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I thought I had pointed that out at the opening of my remarks to-night. The air cadet league is an organization with a charter established for the purpose of forming and operating air cadet squadrons.
Who formed it? And who keeps it going?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: It is a chartered organization. It has a national charter to form and operate air cadet squadrons.

Is it a civilian
organization?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
It is a
civilian organization, yes.

Well, that is just the point I cannot get the logic out of. Is the air cadet movement in Canada to depend entirely on the air cadet league? I do not see who originates the air cadet league and what keeps it going and what connection there is between the department and the league.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The air cadet league forms these squadrons. There are also civilian organizations in the various centres with civilian boards in centres such as Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg and other places, and these civilian organizations get behind the groups of boys who are formed into squadrons. They assist the squadrons, and in addition to the local sponsors there are provincial air cadet organizations that operate under the air cadet league. The league executive is at the top. They have provincial organizations and local organizations, and the local organizations have arranged for sponsors for various squadrons in these localities. These are all provided by civilian effort and they raise funds from civilian sources to assist the squadrons for which they are responsible. The Royal Canadian Air Force also assists in providing pay for instructors as well as grants and capitation fees to the boys according to the numbers in the squadrons. Various other grants are also given for clothing, bands and so forth, and funds are provided

Air Force Act-Cadet Squadrons

for summer camps. In addition, the officers attached to the squadrons are paid by the Royal Canadian Air Force. But the organization that sponsors these squadrons is entirely civilian.

The same question is likely to arise in the discussion of the army and navy cadets. It seems to me that it is a privilege for any boy to be able to join any of these cadet corps. Many of the boys will want to join, and I believe that the opinion of the country has changed considerably in comparison with the pre-war antagonism to cadet training. To-day people realize that such training can do a great deal of good for the youth of Canada, whether it be in promoting physical fitness, in distilling discipline, or in making these boys potential members of the armed forces. This being the case, many of us in the house would like to have from the government an enunciation of policy generally so far as youth training is concerned whether in connection with air cadets or army cadets or sea cadets. I do not think it should be left entirely to a voluntary organization to solicit the minister's permission to form a squadron here or a unit there. The smaller schools in the urban and rural areas, as well as those in the big cities, should have the privilege of establishing cadet classes. In some towns there are cadets in connection with all three forces, but no doubt there are many towns that are without cadet training for any of the forces. .
I can remember when I was going to school we had an army cadet class and I was proud to belong to it, but it developed just before the war that public opinion was to a great extent opposed to cadet training in schools. I believe, however, that public opinion has changed vastly, and the government can give some leadership by announcing its policy as to whether it feels that, in the interests of peace and for the sake of the health and welfare of our youth, as well as for the benefit of the whole country at large, these cadet classes should be encouraged throughout the country generally and not be left merely to promotion by voluntary organizations. I would ask the minister to give us some insight into the government's position in this matter with regard to cadet training in his department as well as in the other two departments of national defence. Can he not go farther than he has indicated to-night in assisting this important movement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
I would not wish to say that the Royal Canadian Air Force or any of the defence departments are responsible for youth training in a general way

or from the point of view of what might be considered part of the health and welfare of the nation. We are defence departments, and it is the responsibility of these departments to provide some preliminary training to the youth of the country in defence matters so that they will be qualified to join the defence forces when they become of age to enlist. Better results have been secured, not in having every boy put into the defence force, but by having units with a waiting list of boys who are keen to get in. Far better results are obtained in that way than by having a unit into which every boy automatically enters, where he parades on the day of inspection and perhaps not again throughout the entire season. In that case morale is low and so Is efficiency. Consequently, we find it preferable to keep the numbers limited to boys who are keen to stay in. That has produced and is producing the best results.
Is the minister interested only in getting boys to join the force in so far as they may be potential members of a permanent force? Is there not a broader outlook than that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: As I have pointed out, we could not take them all into the permanent force if we wanted to. We are responsible for giving preliminary defence training to those boys who come into these cadet squadrons, and they are available to go into some of the forces, permanent or auxiliary; or if they are called upon later, they will have had valuable preliminary training.
Why not have a sufficient number so that you can pick what you require.

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, May IS, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie that the house go into committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Bracken, and the amendment to the amendment of Mrs. Strum.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
In this house, Mr. Speaker, we hear a great variety of subjects discussed, and when a subject is up for debate there is no telling what it will lead to, as we have seen to-night. But there is no doubt in the mind of anyone in this house that the cause of the farmer is well and ably championed. To-night we are speaking on an amendment and a subamendment, both of which deal with farmers' problems. Both the amendment and the subamendment focus attention on farm products as the salient feature of this country's economy. Probably this is truer of the Progressive Conservative amendment than of the C.C.F. subamendment, but both overlook the fact that there are in this country food producers other than farmers. Both the amendment and the subamendment point out that the farmer suffers disproportionately. Without even an analysis of statistics it is very difficult to see how that could be the case, in view of the attention the problems of the farmer are given in this chamber.
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

While we in the maritimes are sympathetic toward the western farmer, because we feel that any benefit accruing to him will automatically be extended to us, I wish to point out that we have problems of our own which are not associated with those of the western farmer. We want to make it clear that we fully appreciate his importance in our over-all economy. I am pleased to see the problems of our farmers being given such full consideration, because I know of no class of people more deserving of support. However, at times it is necessary to apply our thinking on a broader basis. The amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) appears at page 1244 of Hansard, and states:
t That this house is of the opinion that the government's price ceiling policies with respect to farm products are discouraging production of needed food and imposing on the food producers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies.
The C.C.F. subamendment, which I think might well be read at this time to give a good picture of what we are discussing, will be found at page 1651 of Hansard, and reads:
This house is of the opinion that the government's policies permitting recent unjustifiable increases in the prices of farm machinery and of steel have resulted in imposing on food producers and workers in Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies.
Both the amendment and the subamendment set out to prove that the government's price policies are working contrary to the best interests of the farmer and discouraging needed food production. Based on what has been said previously in this debate and on my own observations, I would seriously doubt that the farmer has been suffering too disproportionately. It is true that the prices of his products have been fixed, but that is the case with prices of other commodities used by many classes of people throughout the country. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) pointed out in an interesting talk some of the difficulties facing the maritime provinces, in particular Nova Scotia and still more in particular his own constituency. I feel that his speech ' did Nova Scotia some good, because it served to bring before this house the particular problems with which we are faced, Being at the extremity of the country, as I have said before in this house, we have problems of transportation, freight rates and so on that are not encountered in some other parts of Canada. I feel, however, that the hon. member for Cape Breton South was inconsistent when he continued to advocate that wages be increased but that price ceilings otherwise be maintained. Both the hon. member for Cape

Breton South and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) deplored the fact that the leader of the opposition restricted the discussion to agriculture. I entirely agree in that respect. I feel that it is a great mistake to select any group in the national economy and attempt to give them preferred treatment.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: WThy select the manufacturers?

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Did I?

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Your government did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: It did not,

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The constituency I represent is not generally considered to be a farming one. It is widely and justly known as a fishing centre. But there is much more farming carried out there than most people would imagine. There are many fine apple orchards, for example, as there are in Nova Scotia generally. I do not feel I need spend time on the apple orchards, or attempt to advertise a product which is already well known. Last year, however, the apple crop was a failure. The production of this farm product was down. I have heard some strong arguments advanced in the house blaming the government for discouraging production, but I think the arguments would need to be much more convincing to persuade the farmers that government policies were responsible for the apple, failure last year.
The same may be said of the potato crop in Nova Scotia last year. By the same token farmers generally all across Canada do not blame government policy when circumstances in the hands of nature result in decreased crops. This year in Nova Scotia we are hopeful that our apple crop will be better. Indications are now that it will be. We feel, too, that our farm production generally will be better. But if it is not we know it will not be for lack of trying on the part of the farmers. They are showing no tendency whatsoever to hold back because of the government's policy. In support of that statement I would read an extract from the Halifax Herald, dated Thursday, May 16, under the heading "Acreage is increased":
Ten per cent increase in Nova Scotia potato acreage is in prospect this year according to reports from government farm correspondents. Latest estimates fix the intended 1946 seeding at 24,600 acres, 2,200 acres higher than last year. Four per cent increase in seeding of oats and spring wheat are expected.
Granting that there may be some restiveness under price .control, I do not see that it is in the best interests of the country to focus attention on any one group and make the people in that group feel that they are suffer-

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
ing disproportionately. It is well to consider what would happen to the rest of the country if preferred treatment were given to any one group. For instance, if prices of farm products were allowed to increase, they would reflect themselves into the over-all economy of the country, and would increase the burden on all classes of people, including farmers, fishermen, merchants, tradesmen and so on. They would all be obliged to pay more for bread, cereals, cheese, butter and all farm products.
With particular reference to the C.C.F. subamendment which claims that there is discrimination against the worker, that, too, is not accepted as such in my constituency. I hold in my hand a clipping from one of our local papers which states:
Wage price control policy is helpful
The war-instituted policy of wage and price control, as now practised in Canada, has benefited and will continue to benefit the Canadian worker by protecting his living standards and avoiding an inflationary rise in prices, which *would cancel the advantage gained by an increase in his real wages during the war years and since.
That is found in a paper which has never been inclined to lean over backwards-to use the expression of the hon. member for Cape Breton South-in support of the government.
In my constituency there is a high percentage of people engaged in seafaring. This is a hazardous occupation, and the loss of life is accordingly high. Years in which there are no drownings at sea are very few indeed, as hon. members well know. In fact, to the best of my knowledge, last year was the first in this generation in which there were no losses at sea among crews of schooners in our deep-sea fleet. As a result of the cumulative high loss of life there are many widows. I wish those who advocate the immediate removal of price ceilings would tell the house how those widows, on their small incomes, are going to adjust their method of living to compensate for increased prices. They have no means whatsoever of gearing their incomes to an inflationary spiral. The same thing applies, of course, to people on fixed incomes and pensions all across the board. They have no opportunity to keep pace with increasing prices.
It is idle to say that prices would not increase if ceilings were removed. The very fact that there is such a great pressure against these ceilings is a clear indication of what we could expect if they were removed. If we were sure that the ceilings would not be lifted there would not be such great stress to have them lifted. That the two things go hand in hand goes without saying. There is no doubt in my mind that prices would skyrocket at once if ceilings were lifted, and we would find ourselves in the midst of a violent period of inflation. For example, in the United States where controls have not been maintained as rigidly as in Canada, they are experiencing this condition right now, and are envious of this country's well-controlled economy.
Referring once again to the amendment offered by the leader of the opposition, we find it states that the government's policies are discouraging the production of food. The C.C.F. subamendment states that the government policy has imposed on food producers and workers an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government price stabilization policy.
I say emphatically that both the amendment and subamendment are wrong. Speakers in support of these amendments have attempted to show that because of the government policies farmers are deliberately not producing up to their full potential capacity. I say again that this applies more particularly to the amendment offered by the Progressive Conservative party than to the C.C.F. subamendment. The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Mayhew) and the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver), speaking on behalf of the government, have shown clearly that what the amendments say about farm production is not the case at all.
But if one were to suppose, for the purpose of argument, that the government's policies do discourage production of farm products- which they do not-the amendments would still be wrong. Both amendments refer to food products, not farm products aloner- The word "food" is not used in a restrictive sense. I presume it is intended to include all food products. The C.C.F. subamendment does not state directly that food production is discouraged, but it does imply that by stating that the government's policies impose unfair hardships on food producers.
There is the greatest tendency on the part of farmers, and those speaking on behalf of farmers in the house, to consider food to be limited to farm products only. The definition of "food" must surely embrace fish, which is an important food, as all must agree. The inclusion of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges) in the Canadian delegation to the meetings of the food and agricultural organization in Washington is official recognition by the government of the fact that fish is included in the long-term food programme. Surely that is becoming more important all the time.
We can no longer make the mistake of talking about food and excluding fish. There
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

are many in the house who are not fully familiar with the extent of the fishing activities on the west and east coasts. However, I am sure the house realizes the important part fishing is playing in Canada's economy; While we are anxious to see that the farmer gets the best possible deal, I am sure we can assume that the farmer is just as anxious that the fisherman is given due recognition for the part he is playing. To say, then, that the government's policy is discouraging the production of needed food is hardly correct when one interprets the word "food" in the proper way and reads such statements as have been contained in th'e press recently, and I quote:
Nova Scotia's fish catch increased by 6,034,000 pounds in March over the corresponding month last year. Value of the landed catch to the fishermen was $376,000 more than in 1945. Altogether 26,957,000 pounds of fish were caught with a total landed value of $1,672,000. Lobsters, which gained in quantity by 52,900 pounds, and in value by $134,900, were a big factor in the general increase. Catches of cod, halibut, scallops and pollock all were larger than last year.
I would remind the house that fishermen everywhere do not take kindly to statements alleging that the government's policy is discouraging the production of food when they are doing their utmost to produce in unprecedented quantities and are delivering the goods. They are producing all the year round under the most trying and hazardous conditions. Rather than criticizing the government's policies, these people are grateful to the government for what it has done to assist them to earn a good living wage after so many lean years. As hon. members know, assistance has come in the form of subsidies on ships, veterans benefits, floor prices, trade agreements and so on.
I wonder how serious people are who say they want controls removed entirely and at once. It is reported that in a recent speech at Sherbrooke the non. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) advocated that price controls be removed immediately and completely. I understand from,remarks made in this house that many of those on the opposition benches feel the same way, but I think we should have a clear statement from them as to how far they want to go, on what commodities they want ceilings removed and when they want them removed. Many people criticize, but I think most of them realize what would happen if ceilings were removed. A good example of how the public reacts to this problem and registers complaints while at the same time playing safe is a statement made recently by a well-known Canadian newspaper, the Toronto Daily Star. The heading is, "Wartime restrictions should go." The article is quite emphatic in that, but it ends up by saying:

Except for whatever price controls may be necessary, war-time restrictions should go [DOT]
I think in private most opposition members who complain about price controls feel just that way. They have some local complaints, but at the same time they are reluctant to see controls go completely. The recent strenuous objections from the opposition to the increase in the price of farm machinery and the removal of the subsidy on milk serve to illustrate this point. In my opinion it is doing harm to the country to make the people restive under controls which are known to be in their best interests. Focusing the problem before the public and leading manufacturers and merchants to believe that controls will be removed in the near future serves to retard the availability of consumer goods, since there is every reason to believe that, in the light of the publicity resulting from amendments such as these, goods are being held off the market.
Every reaction that I have received from my constituency has been favourable to the government's policy of adjusting controls and removing them where possible on a gradual basis in order to return to a normal peacetime economy without violent inflation. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) said in a previous speech on this subject, as reported on page 472 of Hansard, this policy is adopted in the confidence that price control and the maintenance of ceiling prices have the full support of Canadian people, and the government does not intend to flout their opinion. If these circumstances are appreciated on all sides and actions are governed accordingly, we shall be assured of a quicker return to normalcy, with fewer irregularities.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to state that I am unequivocally in accord with the principle of price stabilization. During the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne last session I stated, and I reiterate it again, that a more satisfactory approach to price control in so far as agricultural products are concerned would be to establish basic parity prices for all farm products. These prices should bear direct relationship to the cost of production; they would not be floor prices nor yet would they be ceiling prices; they would be prices that would vary with the changed costs of production as related to the cost of the goods which the farmer buys and uses. Obviously the government is not following such a policy.
By this policy of permitting the ceiling on prices of farm machinery to be raised," the cost of producing foodstuffs has been increased

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
for the farmer. The increase allowed in the price of gasoline is another example of the same thing. At the same time the floor has been lowered under the selling price of wheat. It is apparent that such actions on the part of the government is placing an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the price stabilization policy upon the shoulders of the people who obtain their livelihood by tilling the soil.
I can see absolutely no justification for the increase in the price of farm implements. There are many serious objections that could be taken to the raising by 12^ per cent of the ceiling on the selling price of farm machinery manufactured here in the Dominion of Canada. First, farmers to-day are in grave need of machinery replacements for their worn-out equipment. This, added to the increase in price, adds most substantially to the burden the farmer is forced to bear. He must purchase large quantities of new implements to replace his old machinery and must pay higher prices.
Second, higher machinery prices will increase the cost of production. In the face of a lowered floor price of SI a bushel for wheat at Fort William, I cannot see any justification for raising the ceiling on the goods the farmer has to buy.
Third, I question the reliability of the figures which apparently were submitted to the government by the farm machinery companies and which were quoted by the Minister of Finance to indicate increased costs for the implement manufacturers. I question that data unless it was procured directly from the records of the companies concerned and by investigators of the government. Machinery prices have been unjustifiably high for years, according to the report of the special committee on farm implements which sat in 1937.
According to evidence which was submitted to that committee of parliament, and which appears on page 13 of the report of proceedings:
It appears that a small cream separator (under 500 lbs. capacity) can be manufactured in Sweden by a company allied with the De Laval Company, doing business in Canada, and after payment of freight (ocean and rail), duty, excise tax, can be laid down at Peterborough, Ontario, for $17.65. These particular cream separators are sold at Winnipeg for an average price of $44.58. When it is remembered that the freight from Peterborough to Winnipeg is only $1.30, this committee is of the opinion that the above facts speak for themselves, and that the retail price to the Canadian farmer is completely out of line with manufacturing and distribution costs.
I particularly wish to emphasize that last statement:
The retail price to the Canadian farmer is completely out of line with manufacturing and distribution costs.
May I now refer to repeated statements which have emanated from industrial and financial leaders, and may I add that these men are not of the C.C.F. Certainly none with whom I have conversed are sympathetic with our policies in this corner of the house. As a matter of fact, they largely support the Progressive Conservative point of view, which appears to be to take off the lid so that prices on every commodity may go sky-high.
These leaders of industry and finance, directors, in other words, of big business, maintain that increased labour costs are * largely responsible for the high prices of manufactured goods. Certainly labour costs have risen to some extent, but no more than the increased costs of living would justify. Labour, despite these increases, is still not receiving its fair share of the national income. The labouring man, and that includes the fishermen who have just been referred to by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters), who comprises such a large part of this' country's population has always been in the lower income brackets. Too often industrialists have had too much regard for profits and have failed to respect the old biblical counsel: the labourer is worthy of his hire. The small share that labour received from the price realized from farm machinery is revealed on page 435 of the proceedings of the special committee, 1937, on farm implement prices. I think this house and the country should carefully examine that report. On page 435 of the proceedings of the special committee on farm implement prices it is stated that in 1913-quite a long time ago- the selling price of an eight-foot binder sold in the city of Regina was $165. The price itself would indicate that that was a long time ago. Labour costs amounted to 810.21-
I repeat, only $10.21-not a very large sum as everyone must admit. In 1932 the same binder sold in Regina for $276 and the labour cost amounted to only $13.40, still a very small percentage of the selling price, actually just 4-8 per cent.
In every case, the selling commission, freight from the factory to Regina, factory overhead, and materia! costs, each exceeded the cost of labour. Later figures are not available from a reliable source in Canada. But in the United States, where labour in most industries is on a higher wage level than in this country, the report of the federal trade commission, issued from Washington, D.C., last year, stated that the cost of labour in the manufacture of farm implements in the United States has not altered materially in relation to other costs of manufacturing. The report reveals that a

combine retailing in Minneapolis for $638 had as labour costs $46.43, or just 7-3 per cent of the selling price. Referring again to the 1937 special committee on farm implement prices, page 435 of the proceedings, reveals that the highest selling price for an eight-foot binder was in 1921, when labour costs were $20.66. That binder sold for $329 in Regina. Had labour increased 28% per cent at that time, labour costs wrnuld still be only $5.88 more, or a total of $26.54, representing just 8 per cent of the selling price, not 80 per cent.
Therefore I submit that labour costs in Canada, in the implement industry in particular, cannot be the reason for the demand for an increase in the price ceiling on farm machinery. Certainly they are not a legitimate reason for a 12% per cent increase, and until there is placed before this house evidence that can be relied upon to justify a rise in the price of farm machinery, I am unalterably opposed to breaking the price ceiling, the effect of which can only be a demand by other industries for similar treatment. Under the pressure of such a demand the whole structure of price stabilization will be shaken to its foundations and inflation will be upon us with all its attendant evils.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is the privilege, duty and obligation of every member of this house to do everything we humanly can to protect those people who most need protection, the common people of this country who are very much in need of our attention and services. If we get into an inflationary period it is the common people who will suffer the most. For that reason I think it is the duty of controllers, cabinet ministers and the like, and the duty of everyone of us who sits in this house and every citizen of this dominion to do everything possible to prevent any inflationary period from getting started.
As I see it, the constituents of good government are not only the qualities of intelligence, stability, order, vitality and compassion, but ordinary common honesty and sincerity. Instead of going around the country making wild and reckless statements, we should con-

sider what we are talking about. We should reflect that the people of Canada are aware of what is being said and that they expect us to do our duty. In the constituency I represent there are many people, the backbone of our country, who work in the factories, the offices and the shops; there are many widows and orphans, many old age pensioners, returned soldiers, retired public servants and business men on fixed incomes. These are the people who will suffer from inflationary methods, and who, indeed, are suffering from the mere talk of such inflation.
The loyal opposition-I say, the "loyal" opposition-goes about the country and preaches the removal of price controls; that is, they do so outside the house. The United States has gone somewhat upon that line; I do not say that controls have been entirely released, but they have been relaxed to a great extent. Recently the Windsor Daily Star-

Let me remind hon. members that if we have inflation, the industrialists, high-salaried people, and professional people will be able to charge correspondingly; it is the smaller people, the workers in the factories, who will suffer. In 1908 the interests of labour were given fuller recognition by the appointment of a Minister of Labour holding no other portfolio, and the present Prime Minister became minister. To-day we have as minister one who has devoted his life to the labour movement. I refer to the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Mitchell). We also have an efficient department under the supervision of Mr. Arthur MacNamara, who has rendered a noble service to the dominion in the more recent strikes we have had. Between 1896 and 1911 labour legislation enacted by the dominion parliament included the Conciliation Act, establishing the department and providing for conciliation work by

the officers of the department in case of industrial disputes; the Railway Labour Disputes Act, designed to promote the settlement of disputes between railway companies and their employees; the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, providing further machinery for the prevention and settlement of labour . disputes, particularly those in mines and public utilities; the Alien Labour Act, to protect Canadian workmen from the competition of alien workmen brought to Canada under contract; and the Lord's Day Act, ensuring rest on Sunday to the great majority of workers.
The statute prohibiting the manufacture and sale of matches made from white phosphorus, enacted in 1914, was drawn up and passed by the House of Commons first in 1911 but was not finally disposed of before the general election of 1911. The fair wages resolution of the House of Commons in 1900 is the basis of the government's policy by which contractors for dominion government works and supplies are required to pay the rates of wages prevailing in the district in which the work is done. In 1908, the Government Annuities Act was passed. The provision made for the sale of annuities by the government was designed for the advantage of persons of small and moderate incomes who wished to ensure for their old age a certain income.
